bottom_line: Prices are rising fast again, with inflation at 3.8%, and the economy and jobs look strong. So the Fed (the people who set interest rates) looks almost certain to raise rates again next month, which makes borrowing more expensive for everyone.

stories.title: Fed set to raise rates again
stories.real: Inflation (how fast prices go up) hit 3.8%, the jobs report was strong and growth numbers got revised higher. Traders now put the odds of a Fed rate hike in December at almost 100%, even though stocks have been shaky.
stories.you: Loans, credit cards and mortgages could get more expensive, while savings accounts may pay a bit more.

stories.title: Trump calls GDP numbers fake
stories.real: Third-quarter GDP (the measure of everything the country produces) was revised a lot higher. President Trump called the data 'fake' and a 'record setting error' and wants the Commerce Department investigated. It comes before the midterms.
stories.you: When people start doubting official numbers, it gets harder for everyone, the Fed included, to trust what the economy is really doing.

stories.title: New tariff threats on 14 countries
stories.real: The U.S. planned a new round of tariffs (taxes on imports) on 14 trading partners and offered lower rates to countries that sign trade deals. Other countries have already moved their trade around since the first round, and stocks in Europe and Asia rallied as tariff fears eased.
stories.you: Tariffs can push up prices on imported goods, and that's one more reason rates may stay higher for longer.

stories.title: People feel squeezed anyway
stories.real: Polls show Americans feel bad about the economy and worry about costs, even with strong growth numbers. The number of Amazon workers on food stamps has tripled, one sign that workers are getting a smaller share of what the economy earns.
stories.you: A strong economy on paper doesn't mean your paycheck is keeping up with prices.
